images.after: Start with the buyers, then pick the products
images.title: Situations first, products second
images.alt: Flow for planning a buyer's guide: list reader situations, find the best fit for each, label picks by situation, keep the list to four to six.
images.caption: A guide with fifteen products is a catalog, and the reader still has to decide.

items.label: List reader situations
items.text: Write down the three to five situations your readers are in.

items.label: Find the best fit for each
items.text: Every product gets a reason to be in the guide.

items.label: Label picks by situation
items.text: The "best for" labels come without any forcing.

items.label: Keep the list short
items.text: About one product per situation, usually four to six.

images.title: Used picks vs researched picks
images.alt: Comparison of how to present products you used versus products you only researched in a buyer's guide, including labels, evidence and wording.
images.caption: Admitting you used two of five products beats faking all five.

columns.label: Used yourself
points: Show your own photos and screenshots

columns.label: Only researched

images.after: Handling prices and availability that go stale
images.title: Each time you recheck the guide
images.alt: Checklist for updating a buyer's guide: products still sold, plans unchanged, new options, working links, relative prices, honest last-updated date.
images.caption: Keep the volatile facts in the summary table so an update is a single pass.

items: Every product is still sold in the form you describe
Plans, tiers or features haven't changed
No new option deserves a slot
Prices are relative, not exact numbers
"Last updated" changes only after a real recheck
